opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the places where the analogy actually gets more optimistic for AI, not less. People often bring up the child-raising comparison to say, look, we've been "aligning" new minds for as long as humans have existed, and it mostly works out. And the usual objection is, well, AIs might be much smarter than us, or alien in some way, so the analogy breaks down. But I think there's an asymmetry that cuts the other direction, which is that with AI systems we have a level of access that no parent has ever had with a child.

With a kid, you can't open up their brain and look at the activations while they're deciding whether to lie to you. You can't run them a thousand times on the same scenario with slight variations and see how their behavior changes. You can't roll them back to a checkpoint if something goes wrong. You can't directly intervene on their internal representations and see what happens. With neural networks, we can do all of that. We have white-box access. Every weight, every activation, it's all right there.

And even before you get to sophisticated mechanistic interpretability, just the ability to do things like linear probing, or representation engineering, or concept erasure (which is something I've worked on with methods like LEACE), gives you real handles on what the model is representing and how that influences its behavior. You can find a direction that corresponds to some concept and remove it, or steer with it, and check the behavioral effects. That's a kind of control and transparency parents can only dream of.

So I'd say the analogy holds in an important sense: alignment is largely about shaping dispositions through something like training and feedback, the way we shape children through upbringing and culture. And we've done that pretty successfully with humans despite having very blunt instruments. Now we have much sharper instruments. We're also the ones choosing the training data, the objective, the whole environment the system grows up in, to a degree that would be totalitarian if you did it to a child, but which is completely appropriate for software.

I don't want to overstate it. Interpretability is still immature, and there's a lot we can't yet read off from the weights. But the trend is in our favor. Every year the tools get better, and the systems remain fundamentally inspectable in a way humans never will be. So when people worry that we're creating these opaque alien minds we can't understand, I think that understates how much more legible these systems are, in principle and increasingly in practice, than the minds we've been successfully raising all along.

r001.rationale: The response says we can inspect every weight and activation in AI systems, while parents cannot inspect a child’s brain activations, communicating finer access to AI internal states than to children.

r002.rationale: It mentions linear probing, but does not explain probing successive language-model layers to reveal how next-token predictions change across them.

r003.rationale: It does not state that predictions rely on increasingly sophisticated input features as processing advances through layers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the child-rearing analogy gets invoked a lot, and I actually think it's more flattering to the pessimistic case than it should be, because the ways in which AI differs from a child mostly cut in our favor.

With a child, you have essentially no access to the internals. You can't look at their neurons. You can't rewind them to yesterday and try a different conversation. You can't make a thousand copies and run them through different environments to see what generalizes. You get one shot, the learning process is mostly opaque to you, and a lot of what shapes them is stuff you don't control at all, like their peers and their genetics. And yet, despite all of that, most kids turn out fine. Most people end up roughly sharing the values of the culture that raised them. So even the pessimistic version of the analogy is actually pretty reassuring.

Now with neural networks, we have strictly more than that. We have the weights. We can read activations. We can do things like probing, or activation steering, or look at what changes when you fine-tune on a particular dataset. We can checkpoint the model throughout training and ask what it looked like before and after some intervention. The interpretability tools are still crude, I'm not going to oversell them, but the point is that the direction of the asymmetry is clear. It's not that AI is a harder version of the child problem where we have less insight. It's an easier version where we have more insight and more control over the training distribution.

And I think that matters for the specific worry people have, which is something like deceptive alignment, where the model looks good on the outside but has some hidden agenda. With a human teenager, that's a real concern, because you genuinely can't check. With a model, that's an empirical question we can actually try to study, and so far, when people have gone looking for these kinds of hidden misaligned goals in models trained normally, they haven't really found them. You can construct them deliberately, sure, but that's a different thing.

So I'd say inspectability weakens the analogy in a way that should make us more optimistic, not less. The parts of parenting that make it scary are precisely the parts that don't transfer.

r001.rationale: The response says we can inspect neural-network weights and activations and use probing, giving more insight into AI internals than we have with children.

r002.rationale: It mentions probing generally, but does not explain using linear probes across successive layers to reveal changes in next-token predictions.

r003.rationale: It does not state that predictions rely on increasingly sophisticated input features as processing moves through layers.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy breaks down in an important way because we have access to AI systems that we just don’t have with children. You can’t look directly at a child’s brain, inspect all the connections, or make a copy and run a controlled experiment. With an AI system, we can, in principle, inspect every activation and every weight. We can intervene, see what changes, and repeat the experiment from exactly the same starting point.

Now, having access to those numbers doesn’t mean we understand what they’re doing. That’s the interpretability problem. But it means we’re not necessarily limited to inferring what a system wants from what it says and how it behaves. We can potentially investigate the mechanisms producing that behavior.

So raising children might be a useful analogy for some aspects of training, but I wouldn’t use it to establish the limits of alignment. We have a different set of tools available, and those tools could make the problem much more tractable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy to raising children misses a pretty important difference, which is that we have much more access to the internals of an AI system than we do to a human brain. With a child, you mostly have to infer what they believe and what they want from what they say and do. With a neural network, at least in principle, you can inspect every activation, you can change the weights, and you can run controlled experiments to see what causes a particular behavior.

Now, having access to those numbers doesn’t mean we understand them. Interpretability is still a hard problem. But it means we shouldn’t assume that alignment has to be limited to the kinds of supervision available to a parent. We can potentially develop tools that tell us something about what’s going on internally, rather than relying entirely on whether the system behaves well when we’re watching it. That makes me more optimistic about alignment than the child-rearing analogy alone would suggest.
